title: Properties of Acids & Bases
page_title: Properties of Acids & Bases | Cambridge (CIE) IGCSE Chemistry Revision Notes 2021

titles.topic: The Characteristic Properties of Acids & Bases

blocks.name: Properties of acids
blocks.definition:
Describe the characteristic properties of acids in terms of their reactions with: 
metals 
bases 
carbonates
Describe acids in terms of their effect on: 
litmus 
thymolphthalein 
methyl orange

blocks.md:
- Acids have pH values of below 7, have a sour taste (when edible) and are corrosive
- Acids are substances that can neutralise a base, forming a salt and water
- When **acids** are added to water, they form positively charged **hydrogen ions** (H<sup>+</sup>)
- The presence of H<sup>+</sup> ions is what makes a solution acidic
**Example: **Hydrochloric acid
HCl (aq)   →    H<sup>+</sup> (aq)    +    Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq)

- Only metals** above hydrogen** in the reactivity series will react with dilute acids.
- When acids react with metals they form a salt and hydrogen gas:
**acid    +    metal   →    salt    +    hydrogen**
- The name of the salt is related to the name of the acid used, as it depends on the **anion** within the acid

blocks.text: Examples of the names of salts from specific acids and metals

blocks.md:
| **Acid** | **Name of products** | **Equation for reaction** |
|---|---|---|
| Hydrochloric acid | Magnesium chloride and hydrogen | Mg + 2HCl → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> |
| Sulfuric acid | Magnesium sulfate and hydrogen | Mg + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → MgSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> |
| Nitric acid | Magnesium nitrate and hydrogen | Mg + 2HNO<sub>3</sub> → Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> |

- Metal **oxides** and metal **hydroxides** (**alkalis**) can act as **bases**
- When they react with acid, a **neutralisation** reaction occurs
- In all acid-base neutralisation reactions, **salt** and **water **are produced
**acid    +    base   →    salt    +    water**

blocks.text: Examples of reactions between acids and bases

blocks.md:
| **Acid** | **Name of products** | **Equation for reaction** |
|---|---|---|
| Hydrochloric acid | Magnesium chloride and water | Mg(OH)<sub>2 </sub>+ 2HCl → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O |
| Sulfuric acid | Magnesium sulfate and water | MgO + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → MgSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O |
| Nitric acid | Magnesium nitrate and water | Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2HNO<sub>3</sub> → Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O |
- Acids will react with metal carbonates to form the corresponding metal salt, carbon dioxide and water:
**acid  +  metal carbonate → salt  +  carbon dioxide  +  water**

blocks.text: Examples of reactions between acids and carbonates

blocks.md:
| **Acid** | **Name of products** | **Equation for reaction** |
|---|---|---|
| Hydrochloric acid | Magnesium chloride, carbon dioxide and water | MgCO<sub>3 </sub>+ 2HCl → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O |
| Sulfuric acid | Magnesium sulfate, carbon dioxide and water | MgCO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → MgSO<sub>4</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O |
| Nitric acid | Magnesium nitrate, carbon dioxide and water | MgCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HNO<sub>3</sub> → Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O |

- Two colour indicators are used to distinguish between acids and alkalis
- Many plants contain substances that can act as indicators and the most common one is **litmus** which is extracted from lichens
- Synthetic indicators are organic compounds that are sensitive to changes in acidity and appear different colours in acids and alkalis
- **Thymolphthalein **and **methyl orange** are synthetic indicators frequently used in acid-alkali titrations

| **Indicator** | **Colour in acid** | **Colour in alkali** |
|---|---|---|
| Litmus | red | blue |
| Thymolphthalein | colourless | blue |
| Methyl orange | red | yellow |

- Synthetic indicators are used to show the endpoint in titrations as they have a very sharp change of colour when an acid has been neutralised by alkali and vice-versa
- Litmus is not suitable for titrations as the colour change is not sharp and it goes through a purple transition colour in neutral solutions making it difficult to determine an endpoint
- Litmus is very useful as an indicator paper and comes in red and blue versions, for dipping into solutions or testing gases

blocks.name: Properties of bases & alkalis
blocks.definition:
3. State that bases are oxides or hydroxides of metals and that alkalis are soluble bases
Describe the characteristic properties of bases in terms of their reactions with: 
acids 
ammonium salts
Describe alkalis in terms of their effect on: 
litmus 
thymolphthalein 
methyl orange

blocks.md:
- Bases have pH values of above 7
- A base which is water-soluble is referred to as an **alkali**
- In basic (alkaline) conditions red litmus paper turns **blue**,** **methyl orange indicator turns **yellow **and thymolphthalein indicator turns** blue**
- Bases are substances which can neutralise an acid, forming a salt and water
- Bases are usually **oxides **or **hydroxides** of metals
- When **alkalis** are added to water, they form negative hydroxide ions (OH<sup>–</sup>)
- The presence of the OH<sup>-</sup> ions is what makes the aqueous solution an alkali
**Example: **Sodium hydroxide
NaOH (s)   →    Na<sup>+</sup> (aq)    +    OH<sup>-</sup> (aq)

- When bases react with an acid, a neutralisation reaction occurs
- Acids and bases react together in a neutralisation reaction and produce a salt and water:
**Acid    +    base   →    salt    +    water**

blocks.text: Examples of reaction between bases and acids

blocks.md:
| **Acid** | **Name of products** | **Equation for reaction** |
|---|---|---|
| Hydrochloric acid | Magnesium chloride and water | Mg(OH)<sub>2 </sub>+ 2HCl → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O |
| Sulfuric acid | Magnesium sulfate and water | MgO + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → MgSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O |
| Nitric acid | Magnesium nitrate and water | Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 2HNO<sub>3</sub> → Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O |

- Ammonium salts undergo ***decomposition*** when warmed with an alkali
- Even though ammonia is itself a weak base, it is very **volatile** and can easily be displaced from the salt by another alkali
- A salt, water and ammonia are produced

  - For example:
**NH**<sub>**4**</sub>**Cl + NaOH → NaCl + H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O + NH**<sub>**3**</sub>

- This reaction is used as a chemical test to confirm the presence of the ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>)
- Alkali is added to the substance with gentle warming followed by the test for ammonia gas using damp red litmus paper
- The damp litmus paper will turn from **red **to **blue** if ammonia is present
